**February 20, 1952 — A Wednesday**

You arrived on a Wednesday, in the deep-winter heart of a year that felt poised between eras — the old world of empire and total war still visibly present, the new world of jets and nuclear weapons and television just beginning to define itself.

---

**The world paused fourteen days before you were born.**

On February 6, 1952 — just two weeks before your birth — King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham, and a 25-year-old woman named Elizabeth learned she was queen while staying at a Kenyan game lodge called Treetops. Britain was still in full mourning when you entered the world. The flags had not yet fully returned to full staff. The nation that had survived the Blitz was now processing a quieter grief: the death of the king who had stayed in London through the bombing, who had become a symbol of endurance. A new Elizabethan era — a phrase people were already beginning to use — was beginning at almost the exact moment you were.

---

**Athletes were competing in the snow above Oslo.**

The XV Winter Olympic Games were underway in Oslo, Norway, running February 14–25. On the very day you were born, Scandinavian crowds were watching speed skaters and alpine skiers compete in crisp winter air. These were the first Winter Games held in Europe since the war, and Norway — which had endured German occupation — was hosting them with unmistakable pride. The Olympics were back. A signal of normalcy returning to a continent that had been comprehensively destroyed just seven years before.

---

**A war was grinding on with no end in sight.**

The Korean War had been going since June 1950. By February 1952, peace talks at Panmunjom had been stalled for months over the question of prisoner repatriation — a deadlock that would persist until July 1953. Tens of thousands of American soldiers were in Korea when you were born. The war you grew up barely remembering was the war your parents' generation was living through in real time.

---

**The nuclear age was very young and very frightening.**

The Soviet Union had tested its first atomic bomb in 1949 — less than three years before your birth. The United States would test its first thermonuclear device, the hydrogen bomb, in November 1952, just nine months after you were born. The arms race was not yet an abstraction; it was a new and poorly understood feature of reality. Civil defense drills were earnest. People built backyard shelters. Duck-and-cover was not yet a punchline — it was government policy.

---

**America was in a hinge election year.**

Harry Truman, who had made the decision to use atomic weapons and who had taken the country into Korea, would announce in March 1952 that he would not seek re-election. The political vacuum his departure created would eventually produce the candidacy of Dwight Eisenhower — and Eisenhower's landslide victory in November 1952. You were eight months old when America elected the Supreme Allied Commander as its president. The military men who had won the war were now running the peace.

---

**The world was still rationing.**

In Britain, food rationing that began during World War II was still in effect when you were born and would not end completely until 1954. In Europe, reconstruction was ongoing. The Marshall Plan was pouring American money into rebuilding the continent. The prosperity that would define the 1950s — the televisions, the cars, the suburbs — was just beginning to take hold in the United States and was still years away for much of Europe. You were born into a world that felt its shortages.

---

**The arc of a lifetime**

You are 74 now. Consider what that span contains.

You were eleven when John F. Kennedy was assassinated — old enough to remember it as a distinct rupture. You were seventeen when Neil Armstrong walked on the moon, and that achievement belonged to your generation's imagination in a way it cannot belong to anyone born after it. You came of age during Vietnam and Watergate, two events that fundamentally changed how Americans understand their government. You watched the Berlin Wall fall at 37, the collapse of the Soviet Union at 39 — the Cold War that shadowed your entire childhood simply ending, its nuclear menace dissolving into history with a speed that surprised everyone.

In your forties, the internet arrived and rewired commerce, communication, and culture. In your fifties, a smartphone appeared in your pocket and made the sum of human knowledge fingertip-accessible anywhere on earth. You were 49 on September 11, 2001. At 68, a pandemic shut the world down for two years.

The Britain in mourning for its king when you were born had an empire. It does not anymore. The United States when you arrived had never lost a war. Its relationship with that certainty is more complicated now.

---

**What kind of world**

You entered a world that still ran on coal and printed newspapers and sent letters and listened to the radio. A world where the most advanced computing machines filled entire buildings and solved narrow problems for governments and universities. A world where crossing the Atlantic meant five days on an ocean liner. A world where calling long distance was expensive enough that families saved it for emergencies.

The people around your cradle in February 1952 had lived through the Great Depression and two world wars. They were, in many ways, more familiar with scarcity than abundance, with collective sacrifice than individual expression. The world they handed you — and the world you've had a hand in making — is almost unrecognizably different from the one they knew.

That is not a small thing to have witnessed.
